trails.name: Horseshoe Lake Loop
trails.summary: A gentle, shaded circle around the lake — the most forgiving first ride of the season for a green horse.
trails.description: Horseshoe Lake sits in the shade of mature valley oaks and is the single most popular warm-up loop in Upper Bidwell Park. The tread is decomposed granite with a handful of soft sand pockets near the north shore, and the whole loop is wide enough to pass another rider without leaving the trail. Expect heavy foot traffic, dogs, and anglers on summer evenings; the lake is a designated swimming area, so children can appear from the willows without warning. Ride at a walk near the shoreline and keep a calm horse between you and the water's edge.
trails.accessPoint: Horseshoe Lake staging area, Upper Park Road
trails.conditionNote: Wheel ruts from winter storms were graded in March.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: rider on a bay gelding walking the shaded north shore of Horseshoe Lake, oak canopy overhead

trails.name: North Rim Trail
trails.summary: Rolling singletrack along the canyon's north shoulder with long sight lines and steady, rideable climbs.
trails.description: The North Rim is the backbone of Upper Park riding: a rolling traverse that stays high above Big Chico Creek and opens into viewpoints over the Sacramento Valley. Most of the tread is firm, but the two creek crossings at the eastern end cut deeply after rain and the basalt shelves under the crossings turn slick. This is a conditioning ride rather than a stroll — plan for two hours with a fit horse. Riders meet bicycles and trail runners here regularly; CEA asks members to announce themselves early and to step off on the downhill side.
trails.accessPoint: Ten Mile House staging area or CEA Arena
trails.conditionNote: Two downed oaks near the 2-mile mark; passable but narrow.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: two riders in single file on the North Rim with the valley hazy below, late afternoon light

trails.name: South Rim Trail
trails.summary: The sunny counterpart to the North Rim — wider, faster, and the park's best canter when the ground is dry.
trails.description: South Rim runs the length of the canyon on the warmer side, so it dries out two to three weeks before the north-facing trails and stays rideable well into the wet season. The tread is mostly hard-packed dirt over decomposed granite with a few loose, rocky pitches where seasonal drainages cut across. Because it is wide and open, it attracts speed; CEA's standing guidance is to canter only in the straight middle section and to walk the blind corners above the creek. Cattle graze the south side under permit in spring — close every gate you find closed.
trails.conditionNote: Grazing permit cattle on the south slope through May.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: riders trotting the open shoulder of South Rim Trail, golden grasses and blue oaks

trails.name: Yahi Trail
trails.summary: The classic descent from the rim to Big Chico Creek, with the park's most photographed creek crossing.
trails.description: Yahi drops off the rim through chaparral and live oak before meeting the creek at a broad, shallow crossing that horses almost always enjoy. It is also the busiest trail in the park on summer weekends, with swimmers, tubers, and families heading for the swimming holes. Ride early — before ten in the morning is best — and be prepared for dogs off leash despite the leash ordinance. The climb back out is steady and shaded; give horses a breather at the creek before starting up.
trails.conditionNote: Creek is knee-deep and clear; footing is good cobble.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: horse drinking mid-creek at the Yahi crossing, rider in a straw hat, dappled light

trails.name: Middle Trail
trails.summary: A quiet connector between Five Mile and Cedar Grove that stays level and forgiving.
trails.description: Middle Trail is the park's best-kept secret for riders who want mileage without drama. It traverses the canyon slope at a near-constant elevation, so there is no real climbing, and the tread drains well enough to stay open after most storms. It is the natural link in a Five Mile → Cedar Grove → Yahi loop and is frequently used for CEA's beginner clinics because the footing is consistent and the width allows side-by-side riding for instruction.
trails.conditionNote: Brushed back by CEA volunteers in February.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: CEA volunteer crew brushing back trail with loppers, gloves and orange vests

trails.name: Wildwood Way Trail
trails.summary: A short, steep climb linking Wildwood Avenue to the South Rim — a leg-burner on a hot day.
trails.description: Wildwood Way is a purpose-built climb: switchbacks up an exposed south-facing slope from the Wildwood staging area to the rim. There is no shade at all, and the loose shale on the lower switchbacks demands a careful horse. Riders use it to turn a South Rim out-and-back into a lollipop loop, and CEA's endurance riders use it deliberately for hill work. Carry water for yourself — none is available between the trailhead and the rim.
trails.conditionNote: Loose shale on lower switchbacks; dismount if unsure.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: rider leading a horse up the Wildwood switchbacks, sweat marks on the shoulder

trails.name: C Trail Fence Line
trails.summary: Fast, level riding beside the pasture fence line between the CEA Arena and Ten Mile House.
trails.description: The fence line is what members use when they want to move a horse out without leaving the flats. It runs level along the old pasture fence, so you can trot and canter on good footing and keep an eye on the arena activity at the same time. Gates at both ends are wire-and-post; if you open one, close it. The trail floods for a day or two after heavy rain where it crosses the irrigation ditch near Ten Mile House — the culvert is obvious and easily walked around.
trails.conditionNote: Irrigation ditch crossing is dry and firm.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: riders cantering along the C Trail fence line with the CEA Arena in the background

trails.name: B Trail Hookup
trails.summary: The direct link from the CEA Arena down to Cedar Grove and the creek crossings.
trails.description: B Trail exists to connect things: it leaves the arena complex, drops through a stand of interior live oak, and delivers you to Cedar Grove and the Yahi descent. It is narrow in the oak section, so it is a walking trail in practice even though the gradient is friendly. Because it funnels arena traffic toward the creek, it is where many new riders first encounter oncoming horses; pass left-hand to left-hand and speak before you round the blind turn at the bottom.
trails.conditionNote: Oak duff is slippery after the first autumn rain.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: rider in the oak tunnel on B Trail, sun shafts through the canopy

trails.name: Ten Mile House Loop
trails.summary: Open, level loop above the canyon head — the park's best arena-free schooling ground.
trails.description: Ten Mile House is where CEA holds schooling days and 4-H practice: a broad, level loop of mown grass and hard dirt with room for a dozen horses to work at once. The staging area is the largest in the park and handles full-size trailers without backing gymnastics. It is also the trailhead for the eastern end of the North Rim. In summer the loop is hot and exposed by noon, so most members ride it in the early morning.
trails.conditionNote: Grass mown and arena drag completed for schooling days.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: 4-H riders schooling in the Ten Mile House loop, dust rising in morning light

trails.name: Five Mile Flats Loop
trails.summary: Flat, sandy loop under the cottonwoods — a favourite for young riders and longeing.
trails.description: Five Mile Flats is the forgiving sand arena nature built: a level loop of coarse sand under cottonwoods beside the creek, ideal for a first trail ride, for ponying a youngster, or for longeing a horse that needs to settle. The sand is deep in places, so it is a real conditioning ride at the trot. The loop sits in the floodplain and closes during high water — usually a handful of days each winter.
trails.conditionNote: Closed — seasonal floodwater across the low end of the loop.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: young rider on a pony in the Five Mile sand, cottonwoods and dappled shade

trails.name: One Mile Riverside Loop
trails.summary: A short, social loop in Lower Park, close to town and full of neighbourly traffic.
trails.description: One Mile is the ride you can do after work: a flat loop of packed dirt and grass beside the creek in Lower Bidwell Park, five minutes from downtown Chico. It is shared with walkers, joggers, cyclists, and families heading to the playground, so the pace is a walk and the manners matter more than the mileage. Parking is plentiful but not designed for big rigs; single trucks with two-horse trailers fit best.
trails.accessPoint: One Mile Recreation Area, Vallombrosa Avenue
trails.conditionNote: Playground construction detour near the south end through May.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: rider on a grey horse along the One Mile loop with walkers passing, sycamores overhead

trails.name: Pine Ridge Climb
trails.summary: The park's steepest sustained climb, with a viewpoint over the canyon at the top.
trails.description: Pine Ridge is short and honest: a sustained pull up through ponderosa and manzanita that gains most of its elevation in under a mile. The tread is rooty and rocky in the lower third and smoother above. It rewards you with a shaded bench-rock overlook where most riders dismount to let horses blow. Do it on a cool morning with a horse that is already fit; the descent on loose rock is the harder half and is best taken at a walk.
trails.conditionNote: Rockfall debris in the lower third — lead horses across.
trails.photoAlt: Authentic CEA photo needed: horse blowing at the Pine Ridge overlook, canyon behind, rider standing at the shoulder

trailReports.note: Rode the eastern half Sunday. Two oaks down across the tread near the 2-mile mark — you can get a horse around the western one on the uphill side, but leave the green ones at home.
Creek is clear and about knee deep at the main crossing. Cobble footing is solid. Go before 9am on weekends, the swimming holes fill up fast.
Floodwater across the low end of the loop. City has signed the closure at the gate. Reopens once the ground firms up.
Shale is loose on the first three switchbacks after the winter. My mare slid twice. Walk it or take the road around.

listings.description: Nonprofit intake, rehabilitation, and adoption for neglected and displaced horses. Takes in fire-evacuated animals and runs a foster network across the north valley. Volunteer and foster applications open year-round.

posts.title: Don't Forget to Renew Your 2026 Memberships
posts.excerpt: Membership fees are now due. They can be submitted at the next meeting, or renewed online right here.
posts.body:
Happy New Year — and a reminder that CEA membership fees are now due. You can hand a check to the treasurer at any monthly meeting, or renew online in a couple of minutes.

Your dues are what keep the arena dragged, the trail tools sharpened, and the scholarship funded. They also give CEA a credible voice with the City when park access comes up for discussion, and that voice is only as strong as our member count.

If you are not receiving the newsletter, contact Deni Whiting at 530-519-3803 so we can correct your address. Renewals received by March 1 are entered into the early-season drawing for a free clinic seat.
posts.author: CEA Membership Committee

posts.title: Winter Storm Damage: What the Trails Committee Found
posts.excerpt: A survey of Upper Park after the February storms, what is closed, and the work days planned to fix it.
posts.body:
The Trails Committee walked and rode every mile of Upper Park in the two weeks after the February storms. The short version: the rim trails are open with caution, and the low-lying loops are closed until the ground firms.

North Rim has two oaks down across the tread near the two-mile mark. Both are crossable on the uphill side, but only for an experienced horse, and we have signed them accordingly. Pine Ridge has rockfall debris in its lower third — lead horses across rather than riding it.

Five Mile Flats remains closed by floodwater, which is seasonal and expected. The City has posted the closure at the gate, and we ask members to honour it; riding the loop while it is saturated destroys the footing for the rest of the year.

We are scheduling work days for March and April. Bring loppers and gloves and a good pair of boots — coffee is on us.
posts.author: CEA Trails Committee

posts.title: Life Flight Membership: Why It Matters for Riders
posts.excerpt: What Enloe Life Flight and AirMedCare National Membership actually cover, and why riders should think hard about it.
posts.body:
At the June meeting we are dedicating the program to air ambulance coverage, because it is the single most misunderstood line item in a rider's budget.

A helicopter flight from the back of Upper Park is not a medical expense your health insurance necessarily treats as in-network. Enloe Life Flight membership and the AirMedCare Network's National Membership cover the out-of-pocket portion of a medically necessary flight — the latter also includes REACH and CALSTAR, which matters when you trailer out of the area for a clinic or a ride.

Neither is a substitute for good horsemanship. Both are a hedge against the worst fifteen minutes of your life. Bring your questions, and bring a dish — the June meeting is potluck, Mexican food.
posts.author: CEA Programs

posts.title: Mike Mathis Scholarship Now Open for Applications
posts.excerpt: Open to students enrolled in an agriculture program. Requirements and the application are on the Resources page.
posts.body:
The Mike Mathis Scholarship is now open. Mike believed that the kids who grow up doing chores in a barn are the future of this valley's agriculture, and the scholarship is how CEA says so with money behind it.

Applicants must be enrolled in an agriculture program to be considered. Requirements and the application form are both downloadable from the Resources page; completed packets go to the scholarship committee by July 15.

If you know a student who qualifies, send them this page. The award has gone unclaimed more than once simply because nobody applied.
posts.author: CEA Scholarship Committee

posts.title: Meeting Mountain Bikes: The Protocol We Ask Members to Follow
posts.excerpt: Bidwell Park is shared ground. Here is the passing protocol CEA teaches, and why it keeps everyone safe.
posts.body:
Bidwell Park belongs to everyone, and the trails most of us ride are open to bicycles and runners. The protocol CEA teaches is simple and it works.

Announce yourself early and clearly — a voice, not a whistle. If you hear a bike, stop, get to the uphill side, and let the rider pass on the downhill side. Horses spook at speed and at silence; a cyclist who knows you are there can slow down and give you room.

Yield the way the park asks: everyone yields to horses, horses yield to nobody except gravity. But yield is not the same as right-of-way over common sense. On a blind corner, stop and listen.

Finally, wave. Every polite interaction on the trail buys us goodwill that CEA spends later at a City Council meeting.
posts.author: CEA Trails Committee
